correctness.rationale: For arbitrary bounded complex harmonic maps and each positive index, Fourier boundary duality turns the coefficient sum into a two-phase cosine objective. Pairing positive and negative cosine values gives an exact sharp convex upper envelope. Strict convexity of the integral produces a unique positive dual parameter for each interior center and a unimodular Poisson witness attains equality. Strictness of both inequalities classifies all extremizers; the endpoint limits follow from controlled elliptic-integral asymptotics. The actual standalone check verified 15 parameter/index Fourier profiles, five stationarity equations and two endpoint sanity conditions; numerical tests are not substituted for proof.

originality.rationale: The closest relevant primary publications establish the universal harmonic Hardy 4/pi coefficient estimate, finite-p unconditioned constants, or fixed-center Bohr-majorant bounds; their hypotheses and conclusions do not imply a c-conditioned sharp single-index coefficient envelope. Inspected published neighboring results concern a simultaneous-coefficient radius and L1 stability of zero-center sharpness. Equivalent-formulation, broader-coverage, table and implication comparisons are recorded below. Residual uncertainty about historic optimization literature is acknowledged without claiming exhaustive novelty.
residual_risks: A general constrained L-infinity Fourier extremal theorem in older literature could include this specialization under another formulation; the conducted searches found none.
No independent scientific audit has been performed; mathematical statements should be externally examined before relying on a priority claim.

value.rationale: Fixing a natural Fourier zeroth coefficient while maximizing an indexed two-sided coefficient is the smallest nontrivial refinement of the sharp harmonic Hardy endpoint constant. This result solves the entire continuum of center values, all Fourier indices, the exact equality class, and distinct logarithmic-versus-square-root endpoint laws. The exact frontier is not a routine substitution into 4/pi or a narrow arbitrary finite experiment. The strict difference from simultaneously optimized Bohr majorants is specified.
